title: Model method: part–whole
examples: When should I use a bar model?
How do I know which number is the unknown?
Can I use the bar model for multiplication problems?

explain.say: Today we learn a helpful way to solve word problems. We use something called the bar model. It helps us see the parts and the whole.
First, we draw a bar model to show the information. We draw a long bar for the total amount. Then we draw smaller bars inside it for the parts.

items: Step 1: Draw a long bar for total.
Step 2: Draw smaller bars inside for parts.

draw.text: Draw bars for total and parts.

explain.say: Let us look at an example. A class has twenty students in total. Ten are boys and ten are girls. We draw one bar for the twenty total. Then we draw two equal bars inside.
Next, we label all the parts and the whole. We label the parts with the numbers we know. We label the whole with the total number given in the problem.
If one part was unknown, we would use a question mark or a letter to label it. This helps us know what we need to find out.

faq.q: What is the difference between a part and a whole?
faq.a: The whole is the total amount when you put all the parts together. A part is just one piece of that total amount.

faq.q: When should I draw a bar model?
faq.a: You should draw a bar model when a word problem tells you about parts adding up to a total. It helps organize your thinking.
asks: Do I always need a bar model?
Is this method for all math problems?

faq.q: How do I know which number is the unknown part?
faq.a: If the problem says 'some more' or 'how many left', that is usually the unknown part. You label it with a question mark.
asks: What to do if I don't know a number?
How do I mark the missing number?

faq.q: Can I use this for subtraction problems?
faq.a: Yes, subtraction problems often show a whole and one part, and the other part is the difference. The bar model shows this relationship clearly.
asks: Does this work for finding the difference?
Is it useful for 'how many are left' problems?

faq.q: If the parts are different sizes, how do I draw the model?
faq.a: You just draw bars that match the size of the numbers given. The total bar must cover the entire length of the parts combined.
asks: What if the parts are unequal?
How do I show different amounts?

facts: A bar model helps visualize relationships between numbers.
The whole is the sum of all the individual parts.
Unknown quantities are represented by labels like '?' or a letter.
This method is useful for addition and subtraction word problems.

quiz.say: A box has 30 crayons. Some are red, and the rest are blue. If there are 12 red crayons, how many blue crayons are there?

options.show: Two separate bars, one for 30 and one for 12.
options.say: Two separate bars, one for 30 and one for 12.

options.show: A single bar labeled 30 with no parts shown.
options.say: A single bar labeled 30 with no parts shown.

options.show: A bar model with a total of 30, split into two parts: 12 and an unknown part.
options.say: A bar model with a total of 30, split into two parts: 12 and an unknown part.

quiz.why: The whole is 30, and the two parts (red and blue) must add up to 30. We label the unknown part with a question mark.

wrong.0: This treats the numbers as separate facts, ignoring that they are related parts.
wrong.1: This forgets to show that the 30 is made up of two smaller parts.
wrong.3: This only shows the operation, not the structure of the parts and the whole.

quiz.say: Sarah collected 45 stickers. Her friend gave her 20 more stickers. How many stickers does Sarah have now?

options.show: Two bars labeled 45 and 20 with nothing above them.
options.say: Two bars labeled 45 and 20 with nothing above them.

options.show: A bar model showing two separate parts, 45 and 20, placed under a larger bar lab
options.say: A bar model showing two separate parts, 45 and 20, placed under a larger bar lab

quiz.why: The problem describes two amounts being combined to make a new total. We draw the two known parts and the total above them.

wrong.0: This shows the parts but fails to show the final combined total.
wrong.2: Subtracting is used when finding a difference, not when combining amounts.
wrong.3: While correct, the bar model needs to visually separate the two starting amounts.

quiz.say: A farmer had 50 eggs. He sold some, and 15 were left. How many eggs did he sell?

options.show: A bar model with two equal parts of 25.
options.say: A bar model with two equal parts of 25.

options.show: A bar model showing a total of 50, split into two parts: 15 and an unknown part.
options.say: A bar model showing a total of 50, split into two parts: 15 and an unknown part.

quiz.why: The total (50) is made up of the amount left (15) and the amount sold (the unknown part).

wrong.0: This incorrectly suggests that 50 and 15 are two separate totals.
wrong.1: This assumes the parts are equal, which is not given in the problem.
wrong.3: This only shows the calculation, not the visual relationship of the parts forming the whole.
